questions.stem: A country's currency appreciates. What is the effect on its imports and exports?
options: Imports become cheaper and exports become dearer
Imports become dearer and exports become cheaper
Both become cheaper
Both become dearer
questions.why: SPICED: Strong Pound, Imports Cheaper, Exports Dearer. Good for an importer, bad for an exporter.
whyNot: That is what a DEPRECIATION does.
The two move in opposite directions.
The two move in opposite directions.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of inflation?
options: A sustained rise in the general price level, reducing the purchasing power of money
A rise in the price of one product
A rise in interest rates
A fall in national output
questions.why: Inflation raises input costs, prompts wage demands and reduces real incomes, which weakens demand for non-essentials.
whyNot: A single price rise is not inflation, which is a general and sustained rise.
That is monetary policy, which may be a response to inflation.
That is a recession.

questions.stem: Which business is hit hardest by a rise in interest rates?
options: A highly geared business selling expensive items bought on credit
A debt-free business selling cheap essentials
A business with large cash reserves
A business with no customers who borrow
questions.why: It suffers twice: its own variable-rate debt costs more, and its customers, who buy on credit, cut back. Both effects hit at once.
whyNot: That business is largely insulated on both counts.
It earns more interest on its cash, so it may benefit.
The demand side is unaffected for that business.

questions.stem: A business has $400,000 of variable-rate debt and interest rates rise by 2 percentage points. Roughly how much extra interest is there a year?
questions.why: 400,000 x 0.02 = $8,000 a year. Sizing the effect like this turns a general point into a quantified one, which is where the application marks are.
whyNot: This appears to use $40,000 of debt.
This uses 20% rather than 2%.
This does not use the debt figure at all.

questions.stem: A Maldivian guesthouse imports most of its supplies. What is the effect of a weaker local currency?
options: Input costs rise even though nothing about the product has changed
Input costs fall
There is no effect, because the guests are foreign
Its room rates automatically fall
questions.why: A weaker currency means more local currency is needed to buy the same imported food, fuel and materials. Supply shifts left with no change in the product itself.
whyNot: A weaker currency makes imports dearer, not cheaper.
The costs are paid in local currency, so the effect is real.
Rates are a pricing decision, not automatic.

questions.stem: For a tourism business, which economy's cycle matters most to demand?
options: The economies of its main source markets
Its own domestic economy
The global average
Neither, because tourism is recession-proof
questions.why: A long-haul holiday is close to a pure luxury, so a recession in a few wealthy source countries cuts bookings sharply even while the domestic economy grows. Spreading across more source markets is the standard response.
whyNot: Domestic incomes matter far less when most customers are foreign.
A global average conceals the specific countries visitors come from.
Tourism is one of the most cycle-sensitive sectors.

questions.stem: What should a business do in a boom, according to the business cycle framework?
options: Invest and build capacity, while keeping cash back for the downturn
Cut all spending and hold cash only
Rationalise and reduce capacity
Take on as much debt as possible
questions.why: Demand is high so capacity is needed, and the discipline is to keep reserves because the downturn follows. Businesses that spend the whole boom struggle in the recession.
whyNot: That is the recession response.
Reducing capacity in a boom means turning away profitable demand.
Maximum gearing going into a downturn is how businesses fail.

questions.stem: Why do luxury goods businesses swing hardest through the business cycle?
options: They have a high income elasticity of demand, so demand changes by more than income does
They have higher fixed costs than other businesses
They are always highly geared
Luxury goods are always imported
questions.why: A YED above 1 amplifies the income change. A 3% fall in incomes with a YED of 2.5 cuts demand by about 7.5%, which is why these businesses boom and collapse hardest.
whyNot: Cost structure varies and is not what drives the cyclical swing.
Gearing varies between firms.
Many are produced domestically.

questions.stem: Which response to inflation depends on price elasticity of demand?
options: Passing the cost increase on to customers through higher prices
Negotiating a fixed-price supply contract
Improving productivity to offset the cost
Reducing package sizes
questions.why: Whether you can pass it on depends on how customers respond to a higher price, and on what competitors do. With elastic demand, passing it on loses significant volume.
whyNot: A supply-side response that does not depend on customer behaviour.
An internal efficiency response.
A way of avoiding a headline price rise, and its success depends on whether customers notice rather than on elasticity as such.
